references.text: Rachel was jealous of Leah because she was barren, and asked Jacob for children. This is the direct background to Rachel's disgrace which God now removes in verse 23.
God intervened for Sarah and made her fruitful, so that she gave birth to Isaac. This mirrors God's intervention for Rachel by giving her a son and removing her disgrace.
Isaac prayed to the Lord for his barren wife Rebekah, and the Lord heard his prayer. This shows God's intervention in situations of barrenness, parallel to Rachel's experience.
The Lord saw that Leah was unloved and opened her womb, while Rachel remained barren. This is the background to Rachel's disgrace which is now being removed.
Hannah was barren and suffered under disgrace, like Rachel's situation. God had closed her womb but later intervened.
The Lord remembered Hannah, and she conceived and gave birth to Samuel. A strong parallel to how God remembered Rachel and gave her Joseph.
He gives the barren woman a home and makes her a joyful mother of children. This reflects God's ability to remove disgrace due to barrenness, as He did for Rachel.
Elizabeth said that the Lord has taken away her disgrace among people, almost identical to Rachel's statement that God has removed her disgrace.
Both verses document Leah's progression from feeling unloved to experiencing God's intervention to remove her shame.
Both verses are part of the same story about how God responds to the sisters' conflict by giving children to both women.
Shows Leah's theological development from seeking to remove shame to being able to praise the Lord independently of her husband's love.
Forms a thematic framework for Leah's life: from hope in her husband's love (Reuben) to complete removal of shame (Simeon).
